Return occurs within Persian rule

Verse 1 credits the LORD with moving a foreign king. Verse 3 makes the return a matter of choice: “Whoever there is among you.” Verse 5 says those went whose spirit God had stirred. Permission comes from the ruler of the whole region. No king of Judah is restored, and worship resumes without independence. Verses 7–11 count the old vessels to link the new house with the first. The Cyrus Cylinder provides wider royal context without naming Judah’s returning families.

Belonging requires more than arrival

After the exile, written records show who may serve as a priest. Verse 62 says some priestly families searched and found nothing. They are removed from the priesthood for the present. Verse 63 leaves the final decision to a priest with Urim and Thummim. So the ruling is a suspension, not a last word. Lay families with the same problem are listed and not sent away (verses 59–60). The line is drawn most strictly at the altar.
A foundation holds two different memories

The altar comes first, before walls or roof (verses 2–3). Worship does not wait for a finished building. When the foundation is laid, two sounds rise together. Verse 12 says the old men who remembered the first house wept aloud. Others shouted for joy. Verse 13 says no one could tell the two sounds apart. The text corrects neither group, and Haggai 2:3 speaks to the same grief.
Opposition does not follow a simple sequence

The chapter groups disputes from several reigns. It names Cyrus, Darius, Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, and Darius again (verses 5–7, 24). The letter in verses 12–16 concerns the city walls, not the temple. A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. Opposition is the theme that holds these events together. The order in verse 21 stops the work by force of law. It also leaves room for a later decree to change it.
Local builders answer through a longer history

The elders answer an official inquiry in verse 11. They say whose servants they are and that a great king built it. The governor sends a letter (verse 6); a bulla shows how letters were sealed. Verse 12 admits that their fathers angered God and lost it. That explains the ruin without saying their God was weak. Verse 13 gives the legal ground: a decree of Cyrus. The dispute is about who may authorize building inside the empire.
A stored record changes a local dispute

The search begins in Babylon, and the record turns up in Media (verses 1–2). A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. A stored memo answers the charges of local opponents. Darius goes beyond what the Jews asked and pays the costs (verses 8–9). In verse 10 he wants prayers for himself and his sons. So permission brings duties and royal oversight with it. Verse 14 credits the result to prophets, God’s command, and Persian kings together.
Teaching joins study with conduct

Verse 10 gives three verbs in a fixed order. Ezra set his heart to seek the law, to do it, and to teach it. Study comes first, and practice stands between study and teaching. Verses 6 and 9 say God’s hand was on him. The king’s letter then gives him wide powers (verses 25–26). He may appoint judges and enforce both God’s law and the king’s. Ezra credits God, not himself, for the king’s favor (verses 27–28).
Sacred gifts need public accountability

Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek him (verse 22). So he will not ask for an armed escort. His trust does not remove the need to weigh the gifts. Named guardians receive them by weight before travel (verses 24–27). Verse 29 tells them to guard them until the next weighing. Verses 33–34 report matching counts and a written record. A trade weight shows the kind of tool used for such weighing.
Gratitude and fear shape the prayer

Ezra says “we” and “our” through the whole prayer. He has not made these marriages himself. Verse 8 says God will “revive us a little.” Verse 9 says the people are still bondservants under Persian kings. Yet God has shown them kindness and let them rebuild. Ezra fears this small survival could be lost (verse 14). Deuteronomy 7:3–4 gives the law’s stated concern: turning to other gods.
A boundary decision has a human cost

The proposal in verse 3 comes from Shecaniah, not from Ezra. It covers the wives and “those who are born of them.” Verse 15 records four men who opposed the plan. No word from God is reported approving it. The women and children do not speak anywhere in the chapter. The last verse mentions children and then stops (verse 44). Elsewhere the Bible honors Ruth, a woman of Moab (Ruth 4:13–17).
